title: Fat Worm Blows a Sparky
build: original Durell Software release, tape image made with Ramsoft MakeTZX; a BASIC wrapper loads a 190-byte self-overwriting turbo loader at $FAF2 which loads 49001 bytes to $4000

records.c: Starts a new game when '0' is held on the menu ($E51E reads key $23 and $E521 jumps here). Clears the score ($8060/$8062), the frame counter ($8059) and $805B, fills the play area's attributes ($5800-$59FF) with $44, copies the four 16-byte tracker records from $7FA4 down to $7F54, gives the worm 20 sparkies ($805D = $14) and one entity slot ($7C71 = 1, $7C72 = $7C74), and sets its position, heading, speed and scroll values ($7FF4 = $0800, $7FF6 = $0500, $7FFE = $1000, $8000 = $8300, $8002 = $0A00). It also walks a list of 7-byte records from $646C in the loaded game data and, for each record whose +5 is $0C and +6 is $F7, preloads its +1 field with the value at +0 minus one (what those records drive is not established), then calls $AAF3 and falls into the frame loop at $7638.

One frame of play, entered at the end of every pass by the jump at $7635 and by $779D. It bumps the 16-bit frame counter ($8059), clamps the speed ($8003) to $0A, calls the wave spawner $7925 on every 100th frame, sets $8067 = (frame & 3) + 1 (the main loop clears it again at $76CC), runs the frame's updates ($9CF1, $D438, $AAF3, the sound routine $EAA9 which reads ($8056), $B2F4 and the script player $E9E8), copies the byte at $7F43 into the attribute of the screen's top-left cell ($5800), updates the four-bit tracker ($77A0), reads the controls into $8057 ($7C13) and redraws the counters ($7A30). The control byte then drives the worm: 'P'/'O' (bits 0/1) turn it by -$0C/+$0C on its heading ($8001), 'Q'/'A' (bits 2/3) raise the speed ($8003) or drop it by 3, 'H' (bit 4) spins in the pause loop at $7790 until the key is released, and 'G' (bit 7) leaves for the menu at $E508. Bits 5/6 (SPACE and '1', or the Kempston fire button) run the firing code at $76FA-$7788, which needs a sparky in hand ($805D > 0) and a free slot ($7C71 < 18), spends one, sets the animation frame ($8055) to 2 and appends a 30-byte record at the write pointer ($7C72) carrying the worm's position ($7FF4/$7FF6 minus 5, $7FFE) and $37 in +16, with +14 = -($8001) (the worm's heading negated) and +15 = 4 normally, or +14 = $A0 and +15 = 0 when the '1' key - the burper rather than the blaster - fired it.

Called once a frame at $7688; it maintains the four bytes at $7F5A, $7F6A, $7F7A and $7F8A (the last field of the four 16-byte records at $7F54 + 16n) which the worm's pickups increment (the code at $9E81 adds one for an entity of type $F3). Each frame it decrements all four, slides neighbouring values together so a '1' moves down towards $7F8A, and re-clamps every field into 0/1 with a carry into the next field, so the four read as one 4-bit binary count of what has been collected. When all four read 1 (the count reaches 15) it starts the animation script at $E4B7 ($E4FC) and sets $8058 = $FF, which locks the controls; while $8058 is negative this routine counts it down once a frame ($7821) and, either when it reaches 0 or once all four fields have settled back to 0, discards its return address and continues into the end-of-game sequence at $783B, which fills four 15-byte sprite records at $EB97/$EBA6/$EBB5/$EBC4 (type $E6, first field $7900) and then either runs the long animation at $78C9 or prints the score to the high-score display and returns to the menu.

The long end-of-game animation, reached by the jump at $785E when bit 7 of $805B is set - the collision code writes $C0 to $805B when a $F6 entity is hit, and 0 is written there at the start of a game. It counts ($7FF7) down by 2 a frame while blanking four sprite records ($FF written to $EBD7/$EBAA/$EBB9/$EBC8) and calling the frame updates, then walks the signed delay byte at $BAAD towards 0 (up by 1 a frame when it is positive, down by 3 when it is negative), still calling the updates. It ends in the score code at $788F, which copies the score ($8060) into the high score ($8064) and prints it at $52B7-$52BB when the score beat it, then jumps to the menu at $E508.

Two bytes holding a pointer into the $C5xx picture page, written by $7911 during the end-of-game animation. Nothing in the image reads $790F through a literal operand, so the code that consumes it computes the address.

Stores hl in the two-byte slot at $790F (which sits just after the loop at $7901-$790E) and then falls through to $7914 to run one frame; the end-of-game sequence calls it four times at $7868-$788C, loading the three picture blocks $C5B3, $C5EF and $C62B, which are 60 bytes apart in the $C5xx page. No instruction in the image reads $790F through a literal operand, so whatever uses the slot computes its address.

Writes a to the sound parameter $8056 - the sound routine reads it at $EAB3 and the main loop clears it every frame at $767F - and then calls the per-frame updates $EAA9, $B2F4 and $E9E8, with a+3 in a for those calls, restoring a before returning. Called directly at $786E, $7877 and $788C and by the fall-through from $7911, it advances the end-of-game animation one frame per call.

Called from the main loop on every 100th frame ($7650) to add a wave of enemies: if the entity count ($7C71) is below 10 it raises it by 6 and copies the 180-byte template at $7951 to the write pointer ($7C72), advancing the pointer, so six ready-made records join the list at once. It also sets $8066 = $0C when the frame counter's high byte is a multiple of 4, and does nothing at all when bit 0 of $805A is set.

The wave that $7925 copies into the entity list every 100th frame: six ready-made 30-byte entity records (180 bytes, $7951-$7A04) of the same shape the firing code writes, with type bytes $F0 and $F1 and the constants +2/+3 = $64 and +8/+9 = $0A. Each record's last byte is $9C or $9B.

The 16 attribute bytes of the dashboard's colour strip, the 2-cells-wide, 8-cells-tall block at rows 16-23 and columns 10-11. $7A30 gives one entry a random colour every frame and copies all 16 into the attribute file at $5A0A-$5AEA, so the strip keeps cycling through bright colours; the play snapshot's attributes at those cells hold the same 16 values, copied in pairs (some entries duplicated).

16 Spectrum attribute values for magenta, green, cyan, yellow and white, plain and bright ($03-$07 and $43-$47). They are the pool the random colour for the strip at $7A05 is drawn from, indexed by the low nibble of a byte from the generator at $E472.
Returns the byte at $7A15 + (a & $0F), one of the 16 dashboard attribute colours. Called only from $7A30, with a random byte from the generator at $E472.

Called every frame at $7691 to keep the dashboard counters right: the sparkies ($805D) are drawn as three digits at $5439-$543B, the spindles ($805B) as three digits at $5659-$565B, and the score as five digits at $5097-$509B, where the displayed value ($8062) is wound towards the real score ($8060) by at most 3 a frame so it counts up. The digits come from $7B2E and are blitted by $7B63/$7B6B, and $805C and $805E remember the values already on screen; the two leftmost digits of the sparkies and spindles rows are never written here. It also writes a random colour from $7A15 into one of the 16 bytes at $7A05 (both indexes come from the random generator at $E472), fills all 16 with $41 when the entity list is full ($7C71 >= 18), and copies them into the attribute cells at $5A0A-$5AEA (rows 16-23, columns 10-11), the colour strip beside the map box.

Splits the 16-bit value in hl into decimal digits by repeated subtraction with $7B5D: it returns the units digit in a (also in l), the tens and hundreds packed as (hundreds<<4)|tens in c, and the thousands and ten-thousands as (ten-thousands<<4)|thousands in b. $7B63 draws the digit in a's low nibble and $7B6B the one in its high nibble, which is how the callers turn b and c into two glyphs each.

Subtracts de, a negative power of ten, from hl until it would go negative, returning the number of subtractions in a and the remainder in hl. Its alternate entry at $7B5C only increments the count, which lets successive powers of ten accumulate into one register; both entries are used by $7B2E.

Draws the 8x8 glyph for the digit in the low nibble of a, from the table at $CDB6 (8 bytes a glyph; glyphs 0-9 are the blocky HUD digits), into the character cell at hl in the bottom of the screen. It writes the eight pixel lines by incrementing h and wraps back to the $50xx block with l += $20 when h would pass $57, so the cell after the last pixel row is the next character row down.

The same glyph blitter as $7B63 for the digit in the high nibble of a: it is the entry that skips the four `sla a`, so a single `srl a` selects the glyph for the high nibble. $78A4-$78C0 and $7A30 call it with the packed digit pairs $7B2E returns in b and c.

Waits for exactly one keyboard key to be held and returns its number, 0 to 39, in a: the number is 39 - row - 8*bit for the eight half-rows $FEFE to $7FFE, so 39 is CAPS SHIFT and 0 is B. It restarts the whole scan whenever more than one half-row shows a press, and within a row it takes the lowest set bit. Called by the redefine-keys screen at $E593.

The 40 characters the redefine-keys screen displays for a scanned key, indexed by the number $7B8B returns: entry 0 is B and entry 39 is CAPS SHIFT, in the Spectrum's own keyboard order. Four entries are $81-$84 and stand for SPACE, SYMBOL SHIFT, CAPS SHIFT and ENTER, which have no glyph in the ROM font at $3C00 that the printer uses.

Eight bytes telling the redefine-keys screen which slot of the key list at $7BE0 to overwrite for the key it is currently showing: the byte is looked up with the screen's cursor ($8034, 0-8) and added to $7BE0 at $E59D-$E5A6. The values are 02 01 05 04 07 06 03 00.

The eight keyboard key numbers the play controls use, read in order by $7C13, which sets bit 7 for the first key found held, bit 6 for the second and so on down to bit 0 for the eighth. The default set is $06 for 'G', $24 for '1', $20 for SPACE, $01 for 'H', $26 for 'A', $25 for 'Q', $1A for 'O' and $22 for 'P'; the redefine-keys screen rewrites it from the player's choices.

Returns with carry clear when the keyboard key numbered a is being held: the half-row is $FE rotated right by (a&7)+1 times and the bit read is 4-(a>>3). The eight numbers the game's controls use are $06 for 'G', $24 for '1', $20 for SPACE, $01 for 'H', $26 for 'A', $25 for 'Q', $1A for 'O' and $22 for 'P'; the menu tests '0' at $E51E and '1'/'2' at $E526/$E52E the same way.

The 16 bytes the Kempston joystick's direction nibble (port $1F bits 0-3) is mapped through at $7C3D before the result is OR'd into the control byte. The table moves joystick right/left into the turn bits and up/down into the speed bits ('Q' faster, 'A' slower), and the joystick's fire bit is turned into the SPACE bit, or the '1' bit when down is held with it.

Reads the controls into $8057. It walks the eight key numbers in the list at $7BE0 with $7BE8 and sets bit (7-i) for the i-th key found held; when the menu has selected the Kempston joystick ($E868 = $0E) it also reads port $1F and ORs in the direction bits through the table at $7C03, so joystick right/left become the turn bits and up/down the speed bits, with the fire button as the SPACE bit or the '1' bit when down is held with it. Finally, a held fire button is turned into a one-shot request: bits 5 or 6 set $8054 = $FF and $8053 = $FF on the first frame and $8054 = 0 once released.

The entity list's count byte ($7C71, set to 1 by a new game and capped at 18) and write pointer ($7C72-$7C73, set to $7C74 by a new game). The pointer is where the firing code at $7722 writes a new sparky record and where $7925 copies a wave.

The entity list: 18 records of 30 bytes, $7C74 to $7E8F, holding the player's sparkies, the wave entities and their flight state. Byte 0 is the type (entities of type $F1 give the worm a sparky back at $9E19, $F6 ends the game, $E5 is killed off, $F3 counts towards the four-bit tracker) and the writer at $7722 sets +2/+3 = $02, +8/+9 = $0A and +16 = $37 on a fired sparky. It starts only 108 bytes below the boot forgery text at $7CE0, so once more than about three records exist the list has overwritten that text.
The hand-over stub at $EFD8 jumps here, after the two zero bytes at $7C90. It reads the boot flag at $FC00: zero goes straight to the menu at $7F30, non-zero falls through into the forgery warning.

Prints the warning text at $7CE0 one character at a time with $7CB3 until the terminating $00, then falls into the key wait at $7CA8. The screen in this snapshot holds the finished warning: the print ran from the top-left cell $4000, 591 characters long, and left the printer's cursor at $50F7.

Spins reading IN A,($FE) with the top three half-rows selected until any key is held, then jumps to the menu at $7F30. Reached from the end of the warning print and from its own loop; it is the second half of the piracy warning screen.

Draws one character using the ROM font at $3C00 (glyph at code*8): code 1 is a newline, any other code is blitted as eight bytes into the eight pixel lines of the current cell. The cursor is the self-modified operand of the `ld de,nn` at $7CCA, so `inc (hl)` steps to the next column and, when it wraps at the end of a row, the code adds 8 to the operand's high byte to reach the next screen band; in this snapshot the cursor reads $50F7, where the boot warning print stopped.

The anti-piracy warning shown when $FC00 is set, in plain ZX character codes: 12 lines separated by code $01 (the newline $7CB3 understands), ending with $00 at $7F2F. The 592 bytes print as 591 characters filling the screen from the top-left corner, and the entity list at $7C74 grows over them while a game is being played.

records.c: Copies the pre-rendered menu picture and dashboard from $F000-$F8FF to the screen - 2048 bytes from $F000 to the bottom third of the pixel file ($5000-$57FF) and the following 256 bytes to the attributes of rows 16-23 ($5A00-$5AFF) - and jumps to the menu handler at $E508. Reached from the boot flag check ($7C96), the key wait ($7CB0) and $7ECB.

Scales the object's four extent words at $802B-$8031 by the curve table at $6300 indexed by A/2, leaving the result at $8013-$8019. The object renderer $81DB calls it once for each of the two scale bytes in the object's record - the one at +$0D and then the one at +$0C - so every object is drawn from two copies of its extent at two different scales, which is where the game's solid perspective look comes from. Each word goes through the multiply at $811E.

Replaces HL with its sign-extended high byte (so the value becomes -128..127) and falls straight into $811E, which scales it by the same (128+B)/128 factor. Called eight times from the effects code at $ACE3-$ADB2.

Multiplies HL by (128+B)/128 and returns the result in HL, using a shift-and-add at $812D-$8179 and the negate-scale-negate version at $8189-$81DA for negative values. It only accepts |HL| <= 255: any value whose low byte is $40..$FF, or whose high byte is neither $00 nor $FF, comes back unchanged, which is how coordinates that fall outside the visible area pass through untouched. B runs 0..255, so the factor runs from 1.0 to about 3.0; this is the game's only perspective division.

Renders one object from the list that $B300 walks. On entry A is the object's type, B is the record byte at +$0D and C the byte at +$0C, and $802B-$8031 holds the record's four extent words. It scales that extent by B and by C ($80EB) to get the object's two copies, adds $0080 to the first two words of each copy and $0040 to the last two (the offsets that put the worm's own position at the middle of the view), copies the three fill-pattern words $80B6/$80B8/$80BA out of the 4-record table at $80CB selected by type&3, and jumps to the routine for the type: $89B8 for types $C0-$FF, $8ABC, $8BC3 and $8C84 for the other three quadrants. Types $E5 and objects with B=0 skip the first scaling and are drawn from the record's extent as it stands.

The last arm of the type dispatch at $81DB: an object whose type has bits 6-7 clear (types $00-$3F) falls through the cp/jp chain and is sent to $8C84. Its three siblings are the jumps at $827F, $8284 and $8289.

First of the five face passes. It copies one scaled copy of the object's extent ($8013-$8019, the +$0C copy) into the four words $801B/$801D/$801F/$8025 with the middle pair swapped, loads the fill-pattern word at $80B8 into $80BE, and jumps to the edge drawer $8E13, which treats the four words as two points and draws the clipped edge between them. Called for nearly every object ($84E4, $875E, $8A25-$8A76, and the $8C84 arms).

One of the four face passes. It hands the first three words of each scaled copy to the quad drawer $8FF5, which fills the face between them in the pattern at $80B6. Objects whose type bits call for a face on this edge run this pass and $82D0 together.

The companion of $82B0: the same $8FF5 quad drawer in the same $80B6 pattern, but taking words 0, 1 and 3 of each scaled copy instead of 0, 1 and 2, so it fills the face along the opposite edge of the object. Type bit 2 chooses whether this face is drawn.

Face pass on the other axis: it takes words 0, 2 and 3 of each scaled copy to the quad drawer $9579, which fills the face in the pattern at $80BA. Type bit 3 selects whether this pass runs ($84F0, $8AC9, $8B50 and the $8C84 arms).

The companion of $82F0: words 1, 2 and 3 of each scaled copy through $9579 in the same $80BA pattern. Together the five passes at $828F-$8310 are the up-to-five faces that a solid object shows when it is seen from above; the type byte's bits decide which of them an object needs.

A bare RET. Nothing reaches it with any effect - its only callers are inside the unreachable code at $833A and $8A86 - and it was not executed in any of the three captured runs. The eight zero bytes at $8332-$8339 that follow it are the scratch area that $833A would use.

Eight bytes of scratch storage sitting inside the code. The routine at $833A writes ($8013), ($8015) and ($8017) into $8332, $8334 and $8336 before it draws and restores them to $802B, $802D and $802F afterwards, so these bytes would hold one object's coordinates while it is drawn. The routine is unreachable and the bytes are still zero in the play snapshot.

Draws an object shrunk towards its own centre: it averages the two x words ($800B/$800D), the two y words ($800F/$8011) and each copy's x pair ($8013/$8015, $8017/$8019), pulls each copy a quarter of its own length towards the centre, draws the result with the five face passes ($8A12), then puts the saved coordinates back. No instruction in the image jumps, calls or points here (it sits after the RET at $8331), so this is code the author left in but the game never runs.

Draws one sprite for an object of type $F1: it is placed at the average of the two copies' x words ($800B/$8013) and y words ($800F/$8017), i.e. at the middle of the object, and its size comes from the distance between those two averages, which $B797 turns into one of the pre-scaled sprites in the table at $BF27. The sprite therefore shrinks as the object moves away from the worm.

Draws an object of type $F3 from its own state block: the word at record +$0A points at the block, whose bytes +$0E..+$11 and +$08 set up four of the coordinate words, and the routine then jumps into the shared tail at $B36A, which works the object's width out of its first two x words before drawing. When the byte at block +$12 is negative it takes the arm at $844E, which spreads the coordinates apart by a quarter of that byte before the same tail.

Draws an object of type $E1 collapsed to a single point: it averages each pair of scaled words into $8013=$8015 and $8017=$8019, so the object has no length, then runs the four face passes $82B0/$82D0/$8310/$82F0. When bit 2 of the game counter at $8059 is set it swaps the $80B6 and $80BA fill patterns first, so the object's faces alternate pattern as the game runs.

Draws the objects of types $E8-$EF: it forces all three fill patterns to $FFAA and runs all five face passes, giving one solid high-contrast shape. The type dispatch at $8A05 reaches it with `and $F8; cp $E8`, so the whole block $E8-$EF shares this drawing.

Draws an object of type $E0: all five face passes, then the pair of 16-row sprites at $CC0B and $CC6B ($BCF5) placed at the middle of the object, $18 to the left and $08 up. The sprite pair is 24 pixels wide and is nudged left so that it lines up with the quads drawn from the same centre.

Draws an object of type $FA. The word at record +$0A points at the object's state block; four corners are built from the (x,y) pairs at block -$08, -$04, +$08 and +$0C with $40 subtracted from the second byte of each pair, and that quad is filled through $A7D5 with the pattern at $80BE ($AAAA, and again with $FF55 when the block byte +$06 is non-zero). A sprite sized from the curve table at $6300 (indexed by the block byte +$07) is then drawn through $B7B6 at the average of the four corners. In the captured play state four consecutive objects in the list are type $FA, which is consistent with the multi-legged enemy the manual calls a Crawly, though that identification is not confirmed.

Draws an object of type $F2 as a single sprite: it measures the object by the difference between its first two x words, takes the sprite from the table at $BF59 through $B7B6, and positions it from the object's ($800F) and ($800B) words. The midpoint sums computed above the jump are stored and then discarded, so the sprite ends up anchored to the object's own words rather than to a centre.

Draws an object of type $F7 as a single 12-row sprite chosen from four phases at $CB4B (offsets $00/$30/$60/$90) and positioned from the object's ($8017) and ($8013) words. The phase is the game counter at $8059 taken modulo 4, or its negation when bit 0 of the record's +$0C byte is clear, so the sprite appears to spin - and to spin the other way for objects on the other side of the board.

Draws an object of type $FB as one 16-row sprite chosen by an animation frame: the word at record +$0A points at a state block whose second byte is the frame number, and any frame from 1 to 8 draws the sprite at $CA6F while frame 0 draws the different sprite at $CAAF. A frame number of 9 or more is not drawn at all, so this is a one-shot animation such as a sparky burst.

Draws a type-$E5 object - the first object in the play snapshot's list - as one or two sprites. The word at record +$0A points at a state block: while its byte +$1B is under $11 the sprite at $C8DF is drawn first, then a body sprite is picked from four sizes - $CA3F (12 rows), $CA03 (15), $C997 (18), $C913 (22) - by how far apart the object's two x words are on screen, with the object's own size byte +$1C clamped down to that distance each time. Each sprite is centred by subtracting half its size from both coordinates.

Draws an object of type $E6 as a single 15-row sprite at the middle of the object, $08 left and $08 up, with the sprite address taken from the state block's (ix+$0F)/(ix+$10) pair rather than from a table. It is the plainest of the object drawers: no faces, no animation.

Draws a type-$F4 object as a box: the four face passes, the outline pass $828F with the pattern word $00FF, and four more quads through $900C and $9590 built from the two copies' midpoints. The box's size comes from the game counter at $8059 and $1F (5 to 20), and its fill pattern byte $80BE is set to 0 first, so the quads are drawn as outlines rather than as a stipple.

Six bytes of variables belonging to the chain drawer at $8833: $882D/$882E are the running offset and the step for one axis and $882F/$8830 the same for the other, both advanced by $891C as it walks along the object, and the word at $8831 is the object's total x difference, compared against $882D at $890A to decide when the chain is nearly finished and $FFAA should be used. Zero on entry; only the chain drawer and the helpers at $891C/$8959 read or write them.

Draws a type-$E3 object as a chain of quads running from one scaled copy of its extent to the other. It stores the two copies' x difference at $8831, works out a per-step offset from ($8059)'s low nibble times 16 (through the multiply at $D320) into $882D-$8830, draws a quad ($8959), then steps along and draws again three times ($891C), complementing the fill pattern byte at $80BE on every step so the segments alternate, and closes with one more quad. The $80BA pattern word is set from bit 4 of ($8059), forced to $FFAA while the running offset is under 5 and forced to $FFAA again by the closing pass at $8900 when under 6 of the object's length remains.

Draws a type-$E2 object by forcing its fill patterns: $80B6 and $80BA become $AADD (pattern $DD, mode $AA) and $80B8 becomes $00FF, and then it falls into the generic face dispatcher at $8A12. The object is therefore drawn in one fixed high-contrast pattern whatever $81DB copied from the table at $80CB.

Selects the drawing routine for an object from its type byte at $804F, for every type with bits 6-7 set. A chain of compares picks $851C ($FA), $85D2 ($F2), $840A ($F3), $83DC ($F1), $89A6 ($E2), $84E4 ($E0), $8482 ($E1), $860A ($F7), $8667 ($E5), $863F ($FB), $874C ($F4), $BB06 ($F6), $8833 ($E3) and $870F ($E6); types $F5 and $FF draw nothing, and $E8-$EF all share $84C8. Types with bit 5 clear ($C0-$DF) go to the generic face dispatcher $8A12 instead.

The end of the type dispatch: types $F5 and $FF return without drawing anything, and any other type with bit 5 clear that is not in $E8-$EF falls through into the generic face dispatcher at $8A12. The `and $F8` test is what makes the whole $E8-$EF block share the $84C8 drawing.

The generic face dispatcher: bits 2-4 of the object's type are a mask of which of the five face passes to run. A mask whose bits 2-3 are zero runs all five, and each of the other seven values runs a different subset - for instance $828F+$82B0+$82D0+$8310, or $828F+$82F0+$8310 - which is how one object code covers a flat plate, an open box and a closed box. The subsets are the call sequences at $8A25, $8A32, $8A43, $8A4D, $8A5E, $8A6C and $8A76.
The type mask $08 case: the outline pass $828F plus the quad passes $82B0, $82D0 and $8310, i.e. the same object as $8A36 with one face missing.
The type mask $0C case: the outline pass $828F plus the quad passes $82B0, $82D0 and $82F0. Along with $8A25 it covers the two-visible-faces versions of an object.
The type mask $10 case: the outline pass $828F, then the jump at $8A4A sends it into the middle of the all-faces sequence so that $82D0, $82F0 and $8310 run but $82B0 does not.
The type mask $14 case: the outline pass $828F plus $82B0, $82F0 and $8310, skipping the $82D0 face on the opposite edge.
The type mask $18 case: the outline pass $828F plus $82B0 and $82D0 only, so the object is drawn as a flat plate with no side faces.
The type mask $1C case: the outline pass $828F plus $8310 and $82F0, the two faces on the second axis, so the object is a plate turned across the other two quadrants.
The all-faces case of the dispatcher at $8A12 (type bits 2-4 clear): the outline pass $828F and then all four quad passes $82B0, $82D0, $82F0 and $8310, drawn by falling through from $8A76.

The $10 arm of $8C84: face passes $82F0 and $82B0, another permutation of the eight words for $9819, and the closing $8FF5 quad.

Tests one object record against the query point: it clears ($803F) and dispatches on the top two bits of the record's type byte at +$0E - the $C0 class goes to $9BD5, the $80 class to $9BFF, the $40 class to $9C66 and the plain type falls through to $9B91 - returning carry set when the query misses and, on a hit, the record's depth in ($803D)/($803E) and a projected value in ($803F). The axis half of the $80 class, reached by `jr nz,$9C1E` at $9C17 and by the fall-through at $9C19: it reduces the record's +$02..+$09 limits with $908B and stores the depth into ($803E) with the axis value in ($803D).

Four bytes of code, not data: `ld a,l` and `ld l,(ix+$0C)`, the fall-through of `jr z,$9C41` at $9C3B, which takes the value straight from the record's +$0C byte instead of from the reduced limit. layout.json lists it as a gap because neither coverage run took this branch.

Steering leg taken when bit 7 of (IX+$09) is set, one of four that snap the worm onto the nearest board track. It keeps the new heading only if (heading-$30) mod 256 is at least $20, otherwise it falls through to $9F37 (reverse and quarter ($8002)); the heading it writes is $FD or $83, chosen by bit 6 of the old heading, so the leg picks track direction 0 or 128 with a three-step lane offset.
Tail of the $9EF0 steering leg for the case where the old heading has bit 6 set: it loads heading $83 (track 128) instead of $FD before jumping to $9F31.

Steering leg taken when bit 7 of (IX+$05) is clear. Same shape as $9EF0 but tested against $50, and it writes heading $7D or $03 - the same pair of tracks, 128 and 0, with the lane offset the other way round, so this is the opposite sign of lane for the same axis.

Steering leg taken when bit 7 of (IX+$03) is clear (a jump target at $9EE4, so this leg is entered directly rather than fallen into). It tests (heading+$10) against $20 and writes heading $43 or $BD, chosen by bit 7 of the old heading: track directions 64 or 192, the axis at right angles to legs A and B.

Steering leg taken when bit 7 of (IX+$07) is set. It tests (heading-$70) against $20 and writes heading $3D or $C3, chosen by bit 7 of the old heading: the same pair of tracks as leg C (64 and 192) with the other lane sign.
Tail of the $9F23 steering leg: loads heading $C3 (track 192) for the case where bit 7 of the old heading is set, instead of the $3D the fall-through path uses.

Common commit of the steering legs: stores the new heading in ($8001) and jumps to $9CF5, the per-frame projection that turns the heading into the screen deltas $7FF8/$7FFA/$7FFC. ($8001) is the worm's heading - it is initialised to $83 at $75F6, nudged by a random term from ($E471) when an object of type $F1 is collected at $9E2E, and reversed with `add a,$80` at $A3C6 when the worm bounces off an obstacle.

Hit branch of the four steering legs: the heading is reversed by XOR $80 and stored back in ($8001), and the projection scale ($8002) is shifted right twice (divided by four). Reached when the worm is already heading into the window the leg tests, so it is the worm bumping into the track edge.

Stops the worm for this frame: ($8004) and ($8002) are cleared and the routine returns. Reached from $9EED when none of the four direction flags is set, from $9EBD when the object flag at ($8038) is zero, and from $9EC8 while the 12-frame rate limiter at ($8000) is still running.

It stores the change in the distance counter ($8036) at $7FFD, carries the previous value of ($8039) into ($8005), adds the frame's screen delta ($7FF8) to the accumulator ($7FF4) and subtracts it from ($7F54), then chooses one of the three rebuild cases from the sign and carry: $A035, $A1B8 or the body at $9F92. Walks the queued 30-byte tile records of the board strip backwards from the cursor. The other half of the $9FEC cursor walk, taken when a record's word (IX+$03) is 5 or more: it passes the record's word to $A192, which returns its position in the 16-bit table at $6432 (high byte = which pass of five, low byte = offset within it), stores that back into (IX+$02)/(IX+$03) and rejoins the loop at $A032. Tail of the $A0C8 branch (never executed in the two snapshots): it takes (IX+$03), doubles it and loads the 16-bit word at $AECE+2*(IX+$03) into the record's word (IX+$02)/(IX+$03), then rejoins the loop at $A0E8.
Three-byte jump back to $A09E that closes the second tile-cursor walk loop.

Single `ret` shared by the ring walks at $A0EB and $A313; the code at $A185 jumps here when a link in the chain is zero.

Continuation of the $A275 refill loop: reads the two bytes at (HL) into the entry's word (IX+$28)/(IX+$29) and steps IX by two; the loop runs five times at $A294.

Walks a five-pointer chain held at IY: each word at IY+0, +2, +4, +6, +8 is dereferenced and stored into the next slot, then the chain is walked the other way with BC = 4, dereferencing at +4 and storing into the previous slot. Set-up for the collision pass over the worm's own four records: IX is pointed at $7F54, ($80A0) is loaded with the record count ($809F) - four in both snapshots - and the three view words $7FF8, $7FFA and $7FFE are copied over $80A1/$80A3/$80A5 as the start of the frame's accumulated position; those words' high bytes ($80A2/$80A4/$80A6) are what the resolution at $A79D restores into $8033/$8034/$8035.

One iteration of the collision pass: for the 16-byte record at IX it takes the absolute value of the three signed word components (IX+0/1), (IX+2/3) and (IX+4/5) and adds them, then uses the sign of ($8058) plus a random choice from ($E46F)/($E470) to nudge the record's second and third components by one.
