Zeroes the record's three signed high bytes (IX+$01), (IX+$03) and (IX+$05) when B is $2D or more, the test at $A479; B was set from the record's summed magnitude at $A473 or to $0B at $A470. Reached by fall-through from $A47C.

Continuation of the $A47F block - the third store (IX+$05) that the range $A47F-$A485 sets up - and then the quarter-shift that turns each component into a push: each signed component is shifted arithmetically right twice (the depth one keeping an extra low bit when negative), stored in $9A7F/$9A81/$9A83, subtracted from the record's own component and added to the same offset of the following 16-byte record at (IX+$10)/(IX+$12)/(IX+$14). Those three scratch words are what $A3C0 integrates into the camera position and what the push resolution at $A670/$A749 reads.

Conditional tail of the $A50E accumulation (never executed in the entry snapshot): when the depth component's sign byte is negative or at least $14 it sets bit 1 of ($8058), flagging a collision on the depth axis, and then falls into $A568.

First half of the push resolution, entered after the worm's own record has been updated: it calls $9A89 (the overlap test that finds the object whose box contains the worm and leaves its pointer in $8037, its distance in $803B and its screen row in $8039) and, when an object was found, shifts the record's component (IX+$05) and the counter at ($80A6) by the difference between $803B and $80A6 and shifts (IX+$15) back by the same amount. The clamp `cp $FB` forces that shift to between -5 and -1, and $A581 is the reload point of this push - the object-type handlers all jump back to it - while $A599 re-fetches the object from ($8037).

Handler for an object of type $F7, entered from the comparison at $A5A4: it writes $FF into (IY+$0A)+1, sets ($8055) and ($8056) to 8, adds 5 to ($805D), increments ($805B), adds ($805B) to the 16-bit counter at ($8060) and clears the object type to $FF so the object stops being scanned. This is the same destroy-and-count shape as the $F1 and $F3 handlers at $9E19-$9E63, and ($8055) is a countdown other parts of the game use.

Dispatch test for objects of type $F5: it compares (IY+$0E) with $F5 and jumps on to the $F3 test at $A5F6 when it does not match, otherwise it falls through into the body at $A5E2. The five bytes here are only the comparison; the handler's work is at $A5E2.

Body of the $F5 handler: if the worm's own record counter (IX+$06) is non-zero it clears that counter and calls the sound/effect routine at $E4F7 with DE = $E4E1, so this object pays out once per touch, then it falls through to the common exit at $A670. The counter at (IX+$06) is the worm record's own flag in the 16-byte array at $7F54, reset at $A46C.

Handler for an object of type $F3, entered from the dispatch at $A5DF: it increments the worm's record counter (IX+$06), calls the effect routine at $E4F7 with DE = $E4E1, then removes the object - overpaints its graphics from the tail of the board-strip buffer at ($7C72)-30 with `ldir` of $1E bytes, rewinds the strip cursor ($7C71)/($7C72) by 30 bytes, and sets the object type (IY+$0E) to $FF. The same type is handled on the earlier path at $9E7C-$9EA9, which also increments the counter at $7F5A - the first of the four 16-bit record counters at $7F5A/$7F6A/$7F7A/$7F8A in the record array at $7F54.

Handler for an object of type $F1, entered from the dispatch at $A628: sets ($8056) to $11, nudges the heading ($8001) by a random value from ($E471) and sets the low bits of ($8003), bumps ($805D), then erases the object exactly as the $F3 handler does. The same erasure block (rewind ($7C71)/($7C72) by 30 and `ldir` $1E bytes to (IY+$0A)) is used at $9E51, $A611 and $A65B.

Push resolution for the object found at $9A89: while ($8036) minus ($80A6) is below $17 it goes back to the push at $A581, and otherwise it applies the pending depth push at $9A83 to ($80A5) and to the record's (IX+$04)/(IX+$05) and in reverse to (IX+$14)/(IX+$15), then zeroes $9A83. $A749 and $A79D take the same decision on the other two axes, $A7B2 negates (IX+$05) instead, and the unreachable variant at $A7BA skips the $17 range test entirely.

X-axis branch of the push resolution: it moves the accumulated x at ($80A1) and the record's x by the $9A7F delta, zeros (IX+$00)/(IX+$01) and ($9A7F) and rejoins at $A79D. Taken when the object's x range (IY+$04)-(IY+$08) does not straddle the worm.
Restores $8033/$8034/$8035 from the saved per-frame values at $80A2/$80A4/$80A6 and jumps back to $A568 to test the next object in the worm's four-record array.

A variant of the first four instructions of $A670 with the `cp $17` range test left out: it computes ($8036)-($80A6) and jumps to the push at $A581. No branch anywhere in the image reaches it (the byte pair $A7BA does not occur as a little-endian pointer either) and it was not executed in the entry, play or test runs, so it is either unreachable or reached by a computed jump; it is recorded here rather than dropped because the bytes are code.

End of the collision pass: IX is advanced by 16 to the next record and the count at ($80A0) is decremented, looping back to $A405 while records remain, otherwise returning. The same count is set at $A3ED from ($809F) and at $AB1F, so the array at $7F54 holds four 16-byte records - the worm and the three nearest board objects.

Orders two 8-byte coordinate records - $801B-$8022 and $8023-$802A, four 16-bit words each - by comparing the summed first word pair of each of the three later pairs ($801F+$8021, $8023+$8025, $8027+$8029) against the first pair's sum ($801B+$801D) and encoding the three outcomes in the low bits of A. Bit 3 of the result swaps the two records wholesale, bit 2 swaps each record's two word pairs, and the routine then always swaps the second word pair of the two records, after which it jumps to $9819. Called from $8575 and $8580, which feed the re-ordered coordinates into the line work at $B7B6.

Two zero bytes read as the default word by the tile-ring rebuild at $9FC7 (`ld de,$A8C1` then two reads), which is why they are not executed as code; the $C9 at $A8C3 is never read. The other three defaults sit on top of code bytes and are read the same way: $A8BB holds $2922, $A8BD holds $C380 and $A8BF holds $9819, loaded as data pointers by $A29E, $A071 and $A200.

Sine of the 8-bit angle in A, as a single byte: the angle's low seven bits are folded into a 0-63 triangle (rising then falling) and the top bit repeats the same triangle, so the index is $C0 plus that fold, and the byte read comes from the 64-entry table at $63C0-$63FF, which rises from 0 to $FF in a sine shape (every entry is within 3 of round(255*sin(k*90/64))). The magnitude is therefore |255*sin| of the angle, repeating every 128 steps, and the carry on return is bit 6 of the input angle, which the callers at $B414 and $DF07 use as the sign of that component.

Unsigned 8x8 multiply: HL = E x A, computed as eight shift-and-add steps from the most significant bit of A. DE is used as the running E*2^k and the routine starts by setting D = E and E = 0 so that the first added term is E*128; called from $B41D and $DF0D right after $A8C4, so it turns the sine byte into a scaled component (the callers then take the high byte of the product and halve it, i.e. divide by 512).

Projects one component of the worm's position: E is the heading angle, D the magnitude, and the routine multiplies |cos(heading+$40)| by the magnitude with two eight-step multiplies, using the sine lookup at $A8C4 and the carry it returns for the sign, and leaves the two 16-bit results in $803D and $803F. When the product is small (bit 1 of its high byte clear) it calls $A9A2 instead, which also writes the caller's screen coordinates at $8033/$8035/$8037/$8039 and can zero ($803B); $A99A is the entry that flips bit 0 of the multiplier B first. Called only from $9D02, where the results are halved into $7FF8/$7FFA - the per-frame deltas the view advance at $9F59 and $A1B8 add to their accumulators.

One of the four sign combinations of the 2D rotation subroutine entered at $A9A2 (which the camera update at $9D02 reaches through $A926): it forms the add/subtract pair of the components parked at $8033/$8035 with the products at $8037/$8039 and jumps to the shared tail at $AA71. That tail scales each of $8033 and $8035 by a factor read from the table at $6380-$63FF (indexed by the heading byte held in the alternate L register), writes the results back to $8033 and $803B and returns them in HL and B'. This is the only one of the four branches the entry and play traces never executed; the other three did.

Builds one frame's draw list, once per frame, from the main loop at $7632 and from the board-scroll loops at $7662/$78D6. It empties the list head at $EB7E, rebuilds the four board-panel records at $EB9C-$EBD7 from the four 16-byte panel entries starting at $7F54 (accumulating each panel's position, scaling it by the per-column factor from the 31-byte table at $E48C and storing the projected box at +2..+9 and the two drawing bytes at +$0C/+$0D), projects every live record of the board object table (30-byte records from $7C74 upwards, walked down from the end pointer at $7C72) into a 15-byte list record, and adds the four panels last through $AED8. The first instruction loads $EB8D and is overwritten by the next one ($0000), so the list starts empty, and the two zero bytes it then writes land at $0000/$0001 - ROM - so they have no effect.

The tail of the object-table walk, reached only when an object's byte +0 is $FB (every other type jumps back to $AE45 before this): it decrements the object's timer byte at +1 and returns to the walk, and when that byte has already reached 1 it jumps back without storing, so the timer stops at 1. Neither the entry nor the play trace executed these bytes, so what the $FB objects are is not established here - the layout's data gap at $AEC1-$AED7 is code plus scratch, not data.

Ten bytes of shared scratch with no fixed owner. The board code copies five cell pointers into it and indexes them by cell number ($9F95-$9FAD and $A038-$A050 fill it from $6432/$643C/$6446/$6450/$645A, and $A0DB reads it as $AECE + cell*2), while the draw-list builder parks a six-byte pseudo-record here at $AE77-$AE95 - three word fields with the object's byte +0 at +6 - for the corner projection at $AF73 to read. Both uses are live: the last values the play snapshot caught in it were the five cell pointers.

Adds the four board-panel records ($EB9C, $EBAB, $EBBA, $EBC9) to the depth-sorted draw list at $EB7E, each through the sorted insert at $B008, so the panels and the entities all end up in one back-to-front list. It is the exit of the object-table walk (jp nc at $AE4F), so it runs after every entity has been added. Its first instruction still loads $EB8D, the record the panels used to start at, and is overwritten by the next one, so that fifth record is never inserted.

Works out where one board cell falls on screen. Given HL = the cell's data pointer and BC = the cell's offset from the worm's cell (x,y, each -1, 0 or +1), it stores three words into the 6-byte slot at DE: the cell's x and y offsets relative to the camera ($7FF5/$7FF7, held as 8.8) and the cell pointer. It then walks that cell's data as a stream of 8-byte entries and calls the drawing routine each entry carries, through the self-patching call at $AF49; it is called nine times, once for the worm's cell and each of the eight neighbours around it, filling the slots at $8069+6k that the track code at $EB2B reads.

Calls one operation of a board cell's data: it takes the two bytes two and three back from the walker's tag byte as a routine address, stores them into the operand of the call at $AF63 - patching that call - and calls whatever address it found. The byte immediately before the tag must be $F7 for the call to happen; this is how the cells' data in the $5B00-$757E block turns into drawing commands rather than plain coordinates.

Turns one record of the board object table into a 15-byte draw-list record. From the six bytes the caller parked at $AECE-$AED3 (the object's fields at +$05, +$07, +$08, +$09, +$0B and +$0D) and the camera bytes at $7FF5/$7FF7 it computes the record's four projected box corners at +2..+9, copies the two bytes that tell the drawing code how to draw it into +$0C/+$0D, takes the object's byte +0 into the type byte at +$0E, and inserts the record with $B008. A $FF among those bytes makes it drop the record (nothing is drawn) and $0C/$F7 are controls; the object's own pointer is written into the record by the caller at $AEA0.

Inserts the 15-byte draw-list record IX into the list whose head lives at $EB7E, keeping the back-to-front order that the ranking at $B045 asks for: it walks the list and inserts IX after the last record it belongs behind, or at the head when the list is empty, restarting the walk from the head whenever the ranking says the new record sorts later than the one being looked at. Records whose type byte at +$0E is $FA - the board panels - are stepped over without being compared. Every addition to the frame's draw list goes through here: entities from $AFFB and the four panels from $AED8.

Ranks two draw-list records to decide which of them is drawn first: it compares the two bytes at +$0C/+$0D, then the four projected box corners at +2..+9 as signed 8.8 values. It returns Z when the two records rank the same (the list insert then leaves the older one where it is), C when IX belongs after IY, and neither when IX belongs before IY; if the boxes cannot be separated it hands over to $B0A5 and the tie-breaks at $B2C8.

The second half of the record ranking: the full sign-aware comparison of two records' projected boxes and of their +$0C/+$0D bytes, laid out as eight paths (at $B0E6, $B10C, $B137, $B168, $B1B9, $B246) according to which of the corner values are negative. It is what actually separates two boxes that overlap on the screen but sit at different depths, and it returns the ranking in Z and C to the caller at $B008.

Breaks a tie between two records whose boxes could not be separated: it reads the other record's type byte at +$0E, uses its top two bits to pick one of the three tails at $B2DB/$B2E4/$B2EC, and lets the $30 bits of the type choose which of the +$0C/+$0D bytes decides the order. Reached from the jp m sites inside $B045 and $B0A5, so records that occupy the same piece of screen are ordered by these bytes rather than by their geometry.

The tie-break tail for a record whose type byte has bits 5-4 set to $30: it compares (ix+$0D) with (iy+$0C) and complements the carry, then decrements the type byte in E so that Z says whether the type was 1; the ranking goes back to the caller in C and Z. Neither the entry nor the play trace executed it, so this is the one of the three tie-break cases this image was not seen to take.

The two remaining tie-break tails, and where the third code range begins. Entered here when the other record's type byte has its $30 bits below $20: it compares (iy+$0D) with (ix+$0C); entered at $B2EC when the type's top two bits are $00 or $C0: it compares (iy+$0D) with (ix+$0D). Both leave the ranking in the carry flag, with Z set when the type byte was 1, and both return to the list ranking at $B2C8.

Draws the frame: it walks the sorted draw list from the head at $EB7E and hands each record to $81DB, which dispatches on the record's type byte at +$0E to the routine that knows how to draw that object - board panel fill, track segment, worm, Sputnik, Crawly. For each record it loads the four projected box words into $802B-$8031 and passes the bytes at +$0C/+$0D and the type byte, having first reset the blitter's leftmost/rightmost column bookkeeping $80C6/$80C8 to $0040/$FFC0. Called from the main loop at $7668 and from the board-scroll loops at $78E7/$7907/$791D.

Returns HL*1509 + $29 in HL, built with shifts and adds on a copy of the input in BC. Its only two callers, at $EB5A/$EB64, pass it a word read out of one of the nine cell work slots and use the result as an offset added to the position at $801B/$801D, with (result & 7)+7 handed on as a height to $B9F2. What the 1509 counts - a table stride or a board unit - is not established from this code.

Draws one draw-list record as a shaped body with six limb strokes, oriented by the object's own angle bytes: $8023 is the facing, $8024-$8026 are read as six 4-bit limb angles, $8021 = 7 selects the variant at $B4E0, and the body's width is the difference between two of the record's projected box values ($801F - $801B) kept at $802F. The limbs go through $B491 (angle to screen point) and $B5AF (draw the limb), the body is filled through $B7B6, and the body outline is turned with the angle lookups at $A8C4/$A8D8. Reached by the jp from the type dispatcher's $F3 case at $844B/$847F, once per visible object of that type.

Turns one limb angle into a screen point. It looks up ($8023 + the caller's angle offset) in the sine table at $6380 through $A8C4, multiplies that by $8030 (one and a half times the body width) with $A8D8, and adds the body centre at $802B/$802D; it then repeats with the angle shifted by $40 (a quarter turn) for the other axis. It returns the point in DE (first axis) and BC (second axis, with the body width $802F in B), which is what $B5AF needs to draw the limb.

Entry to the strip plotter for the case where the count the caller put in A is under $15: it swaps in the alternate set, picks the band data for that length from the pointer table at $BF59 (index in A, entry read as A*2) and falls through into $B7DB to draw. The position in HL/DE and the row count in B are used exactly as at $B7E3, so a caller can choose between data it points at itself and a length-indexed strip.

Entry that draws with the alternate accumulator forced to $FF (xor a / dec a / ex af,af') before falling into the kernel at $B7E3, which selects the wide form of the strip (three bytes per row instead of two). Used by the object and worm drawing at $BC88, $BCBC, $BCD4 and $BCFE/$BD0E for the data at $C75F-$C8DE and $CC0B/$CC6B.

Draws one strip of a board object into the 256x128-pixel board bitmap at $F000 (32 bytes per row, the buffer the panel and line plotters share). HL and DE are the position -- the low byte of HL is the row and the low byte of DE the pixel column, old H is discarded, and the two high bytes only carry a sign, so H and D must be $00 or $FF -- B is the number of rows, and the alternate HL points at the strip data. Each row writes 2 bytes (16 pixels), 3 bytes (24 pixels, when the caller set the flag) or 4 bytes when the position is not byte-aligned; every buffer byte is merged with a mask byte and a pattern byte, buffer = (buffer|mask)^pattern, the unaligned rows taking pre-shifted copies of the shape from the pages at $5A00 + (column&7)*256, and the row stride constants $001D/$001E/$001F plus the bytes just written make exactly 32, so each row starts under the previous one. Store opcodes ($B8A4/$B8AD/$B8B6 copied from $B8D5/$B8F7/$B918/$B92A, and $B992/$B99B from $B9BA/$B9DB/$B9ED in the other path) are set to $77 or $00 in the prologue and the side-clipping code, which is how the strip is cut off at the left and right edges; a row count of 0, a position more than one row off the top or bottom, or a run reaching past the end returns without drawing. Called from $863B/$8663/$86A5/$870B/$8748 (the object drawers), $B504/$B559/$B5AB (the strips around the player) and $BCA4 ($BB06's board view).

Takes a single pixel back out of the board bitmap: it forms the address from HL/DE as $B7E3 does, reads the mask at $8F08 + (E&7) and ANDs it into the byte there, clearing the bit for that pixel column. It does nothing unless the position is inside the bitmap (DE high byte $00, HL high byte $00 and row under $80), so it only erases in the lower half. Called four times from $BC28/$BC34/$BC40/$BC4C to take the four marks of the object $BB06 draws off the bitmap again, and once from $EB76.

Walks a board-outline command table at (BC) and draws each segment by ordering its corners and calling $9819. A command is five bytes: two signed deltas that move the pen at $8023/$8025 (each scaled by 4, its sign from the carry of the second add), then two packed bytes that give the segment's far end and the other corner as offsets of 0..56 in steps of 8 from the pen (bits 1-3 of the byte scaled by 8, bit 0 the sign), and a first byte with bit 0 set restores the pen and the far corner from $801B-$8021 before the command runs. A zero first byte ends the table; the two tables it is used with are $BAAE and $BAF9.

Reads the current table byte and returns ($8025) plus the packed offset it carries: bits 1-3 of the byte are the size (times 8) and bit 0 picks the sign. It does not advance the table pointer, so the outline plotter at $BA19 can call it for both ends of the segment.

The same packed-offset helper as $BA8A but based on ($8023): it shifts the byte right four times first, so it reads the high nibble of the byte the caller passes and returns ($8023) plus bits 1-3 of that nibble times 8, with bit 0 as the sign.

One signed byte: how far the view has moved from the top of the board, with bit 7 the sign. Written at $7614 and $7901, read at $78EF and here at $BB0C/$BB30, which move the view's row coordinates ($8017/$8019) by it and flip its sign once the view reaches the top; $BCD7 uses it as a flag and $BD12/both outline paths use its low bits.

One of the two command tables the outline plotter at $BA19 walks (the other is at $BAF9): five-byte commands of two signed deltas (in units of 4 bitmap columns/rows for the pen) followed by two packed bytes for the segment's far end, ending with the $00 byte at $BAF8. Read by $BB5F, which passes it to $BA19 with the pen at $8023/$8025; the stored deltas ($02, $F2, $20, $05, $45, $29, $67, $FC ...) are scaled by four when used, so each command moves the pen over a large part of the 256-pixel-wide bitmap and the table describes a few long board edges.

The second board-outline command table in the same five-byte format as $BAAE, shorter (it ends at the $00 at $BB05). Read at $BCEF, which jumps to $BA19 with it after setting the pen to x=$007F and y=($BAAD) with bit 7 cleared and the dither mask ($80BE) to $AA, so this is the outline drawn when the offset byte at $BAAD is set.

Draws the board view for the frame and then the object on top of it. When the signed offset byte at $BAAD is set it walks the coordinate pairs at $8017/$8019 and $8023/$8025 by it (flipping the sign of the offset when the view has reached the top of the board) and plots the board outline from the script at $BAAE through $BA19; it then calls the dithered edge filler at $8E13 six times, each time rebuilding the corner copies at $801B-$8029 from the pairs at $8013-$8019 moved 1-3 units apart and setting the mask byte ($80BE) to $AA, $80, $FF, $00, $55 and $00 in turn. It ends by taking four pixels back off the bitmap with $B9F2 and drawing the strips at $C75F or $C7C5 (chosen by bit 0 of the level byte ($8059)), $C82B, $C87F and $C8AF at the midpoint of the two pairs at $8013-$8019, and -- when the offset is set -- plotting the second outline script at $BAF9 through $BA19. Entered by a jump from $89FB.

Draws the two 16-row strips built at $CC0B and $CC6B, the second at the same row but 24 pixels (three bytes) further along, using the wide (three-byte) form of the plotter. Called from $8518, which hands it the row in HL and the column in DE, so this is the pair of sprites that make up the object the player is looking at in its current orientation.

Rebuilds the two 96-byte strip buffers at $CC0B and $CC6B: it fills $CC0B-$CCCA with $FF and then has $BD3E plot out of two compressed outlines, the one at $CCD5 twice into $CC0B (once with each half of the word it was called with as the band mask) and the one at $CD6B once into $CC6D, using the band-mask table at $CCCB to choose which of the seven bands of each pass are plotted. It is called with the level word at $8059 from $75E4 and again from $DEE3, so the object's strips are rebuilt when the level changes.

Plots a compressed outline into the buffer the caller has put in the alternate DE from the stream the caller has put in the alternate HL: the caller's index in A selects a seven-bit band mask from the table at $CCCB, and each of seven passes takes one bit of that mask and, when it is set, a count followed by that many (offset, mask) byte pairs which are XORed into the destination at destination+offset. Returns when the seven passes are done.

Three bytes holding a word plus one: $75D8 and $75DC both store BC here (at $BD6C and again at $BD6D, overlapping by a byte) along with the level copy at $8059, and the routine at $DEB8-$DEE0 reads and writes the three bytes individually. No other code in $4000-$EFFF refers to them, and a read of $BD6C just before $75D8 writes it would see whatever the previous game left there.

One of the five behaviour handlers the object system selects for the worm from the level byte at $8059 (the chain at $EBBF-$EBDB, and also reached by call from $AF63). IX is HL, the script record: it adds the signed delta in the script byte to the object's field +$07, clamps the result to the ceiling in the next script byte, and when the field reaches that ceiling it moves the object on to the handler at $BD90 by writing it into +$04/+$05. Its code continues to $BD8F, and the two bytes at $BD78-$BD79 (`ld a,$FF`) are the clamp value, which is why the coverage runs never executed them.

The next state after $BD6F: it ramps the object's field +$07 down toward the floor held in the script (never below it) and, when it arrives, sets the handler to $BD6F again -- or, if the object's type byte at +$0D is $F4, to $BE07, seeding the object's first field from the timer byte at $E471. Also the handler address stored at $BD86/$BEC7 and used by the level chain at $EBC6.

Handler that turns the object's script byte into a position: it scales the word at $8059 by the shift count in the script (shifting right or left for a positive or negative count), runs the result through the projection helpers at $A8C4/$A8D8 with the two object fields at +$02 and +$03, and stores what comes back in the object's field +$07. Selected for the worm by the level chain at $EBCD.

Handler that counts a timer down in the script byte and, when it reaches zero, appends a new record to the list at ($7C72): type $F3, a position from ($8049)+2 and ($804A)+2, a further position derived from the spawner's fields +$09..+$0C, an attribute of $0A or $0E chosen by ($805A)/($8059), the fields +$07 and +$07+$12 of the spawner, the three timer/level bytes at $E46F-$E471, a colour and counters, and finally the new record's handler set to $BD90 and ($7C72) advanced by 6. The number of records is capped at 12 and by the counter at ($8066); reached from $BDBD while walking the level chain at $EBD4.

Handler that paces the object: it stores $20 or $50 (chosen by the level byte at $805B) in the object's field +$15 and, unless the timer byte at $D42B is set, counts the script byte down from $63 (99 frames), each pass moving the object's field +$0B a quarter of the way to the target held in the next script byte and keeping its second field mirrored as ($0C) = $C0 - ($0B); when the count expires it takes a new target from the timer byte at $E470, and the other tail path takes a value from $E471. Selected by the level chain at $EBDB.

25 little-endian pointers indexed by a strip's row count (the count is clamped to $14 = 20 before use): entry n is the start of the band data for a strip n rows long, and the entries grow as n(n+1)/2 records, so the strips are packed triangle-wise into the data at $BFBD. Read by the entry at $B7AE (`ld hl,$BF27`), which passes the value to $B7D0.

The same kind of 25-entry table as $BF27, but its entries point into the second strip at $C2F1 for the short lengths and at $C5B3 (four identical entries) for lengths 21 and over. Read by the entry at $B7CE, which is where a caller plotting by row count through $B7CC arrives.

A third 25-entry pointer table of exactly the same form, identical to $BF27 for lengths 0-17 and then pointing at $C4D5/$C541/$C53B and four times $C5B3 for lengths 18-24. No instruction in $757F-$EFFF loads $BF8B or computes it, so on this image nothing reads this table; it is recorded because the bytes are unambiguously a table of the same shape.

820 bytes of strip data for the plotter at $B7E3, four bytes per record -- an OR byte and an XOR byte for each of the two bitmap bytes a row writes, so one record paints a 16-pixel-wide row. The records are packed triangle-wise (the data for a strip of n rows starts n(n+1)/2 records in), which is what the table at $BF27 relies on. The values ($80/$80, $C0/$C0, $7C/$64, $3F/$28 ...) are one or two bits per byte, so the strips come out as fine broken lines.

A second strip of four-byte records in exactly the form of $BFBD, 193 records from here to $C5B2 and indexed by the table at $BF59. Its first records are the same pattern as $BFBD's (80 80, then C0 80 where $BFBD has C0 C0), so it is the same family of strips for a second shape or colour.

Three 60-byte strips of 10 rows, six bytes per row (three OR/XOR pairs = a 24-pixel-wide row) at $C5B3, $C5EF and $C62B. Loaded into the self-modified operand at $790F by the calls at $7868/$7871/$787A/$7880/$7886 and from $D871/$DE2A/$DE0C/$DE13, i.e. stored in the object templates that $7911 copies to $7951, so these are the sprites of the objects the game spawns; the first bytes ($00,$00,$00...) show their top rows are empty.

Sixteen four-byte records read by the drawing routine at $B5AF. The routine indexes them with $C667 + (C&$3C), mirrors the index when bit 7 of C is set and negates the first byte when bit 6 is set, and uses the third byte of the record as a further index into the two-byte records at $C6A7 (`sla a; add a,$40`), so a record is a step, a limit, a data index and a count for walking one arc: the third byte grows like a square ($00, $08, $10, $17, $1E, ... $54) and the fourth rises then falls, so the sixteen records cover a quarter turn.

184 bytes = 92 records of two bytes (OR byte, XOR byte) for the one-byte-per-row form of the plotter, addressed as $C6A7 + 2*(the third byte of the record at $C667) by the routine at $B5E4, which plots one record per pass. The values are again isolated mask bits ($C0/$40, $60/$20, $08/$08), so this is the shape data for a long diagonal curve through the board bitmap.

Two strips of 17 rows, six bytes per row (102 bytes each) at $C75F and $C7C5, drawn through the flagged entry $B7E0 by $BB06 with B=$11. $BB06 chooses between them on bit 0 of the level byte at $8059, so they are one shape and its mirror image; the first byte is $00 and the records proper start at $C760.

An 84-byte strip of 21 rows, four bytes per row, drawn from $BB06 at the midpoint of the pairs at $8013-$8019 with B=$15 through $B7E3 (the unflagged, two-byte-per-row form). Its records are mostly $00/$7F/$FF halves with the masks $80 and $7F, so it paints a long, mostly solid broken line.

Two strips of 8 rows, six bytes per row (48 bytes each) at $C87F and $C8AF, drawn from $BB06 with B=$08 through the flagged entry $B7E0. Their patterns ($EF/$0F/$D9/$D9/$BC/$BC ...) are three bytes of interleaved bits, so this is the dithered end of the shape whose middle $C82B draws.

A run of nine strips of four bytes per row, each a different length, tiling the 528 bytes to $CAEE: 13 rows at $C8DF (drawn from $867C), 22 at $C913, 11 at $C96B, 18 at $C997, 9 at $C9DF, 15 at $CA03, 12 at $CA3F, 16 at $CA6F and 16 at $CAAF. The four readers in the $86D9-$86FA chain pick 12, 15, 18 or 22 rows according to the object's length (the span between $8013 and $8015, clamped by the record's +$1C), the two readers at $864E/$8654 pick the 16-row pair on a test of the object's script byte, and $867C takes the 13-row one; the two odd lengths, 11 rows at $C96B and 9 at $C9DF, are the ones no code in $757F-$EFFF loads directly (the shapes may also be reached from the object records copied into RAM at $7Cxx).

Four short strips of four bytes per row back to back: 6 rows at $CAEF (drawn by $B5A5), 7 at $CB07 ($B553), 5 at $CB23 and 5 at $CB37 (the pair $B4E5 selects between on bit 0 of the level byte). The 5-7 row patterns are the near end of the same family as $CB4B, i.e. the small solid pieces of the player's view.

192 bytes of 12-row strips of four bytes per row, four of them at $CB4B, $CB7B, $CBAB and $CBDB. $862B adds $00, $30 or $60 to $CB4B depending on bits 0 and 1 of the object's direction byte and plots the 12 rows there, so three of the four are the player's view in three of its four orientations; the fourth at $CBDB is not referenced from any code between $757F and $EFFF.

Two 96-byte buffers of six-byte rows, the strips $BCF5 draws. $BD12 fills the 192 bytes from $CC0B with $FF and then paints the compressed outline at $CCD5 into $CC0B (twice, with the two halves of the level word as band masks) and the outline at $CD6B into $CC6D, so these bytes are built rather than stored; $BCF5 reads them back through the flagged plotter entry $B7E0.

Ten bytes ($10, $DA, $44, $48, $8A, $28, $20, $5A, $00, $08) indexed by the value $BD12 is called with -- the low byte of the level word at $8059 -- and read at $BD42 in $BD3E, whose seven passes each take one bit off the byte with `sla c`, so each byte is a seven-bit mask selecting which of the seven outline bands are painted for that level. The length of ten is inferred from the ten level values $FF-$F6 the handler chain at $EBBF uses; no other reader was found.

150 bytes read by $BD3E when $BD12 rebuilds the game's strip buffers: a count followed by (offset, mask) byte pairs that XOR the mask into the destination at destination+offset, one run of passes per enabled band. The data is a chain of small offsets (04 07 03 09 FC 0D 01 0F F8 06 ...), so it is the run-length description of one outline in the buffer's own byte coordinates.

The second of the two compressed outlines $BD12 feeds to $BD3E (into $CC6D instead of $CC0B), 75 bytes in the same count-and-pairs form as $CCD5. Nothing else reads it, and the glyph block the screen routine at $7B63 copies from starts at $CDB6.

Ten 8-byte glyphs (80 bytes, $CDB6-$CE05), each byte one screen pixel row. The routine at $7B63 takes A, reduces it to A*8 masked with $78, and copies eight bytes from $CDB6 + A into the screen, stepping the pixel row on by $100 per byte and forcing the address into $50xx once bit 3 of the high byte is set, so these are the 8x8 stamps the display is assembled from. Its ten callers are at $78A7/$78AE/$78BC, $7AAE/$7AB5/$7AE6/$7AED/$7AFD and $7B1C/$7B23.

Four zero bytes used as two words by the routine that starts at $CE0A, which reads them at $CE0A and $CE1A and writes them at $CE14 and $CE25 -- the only variables at the very end of this range. No other code in $757F-$EFFF refers to them, and both words are always written together, so they are a saved pair.
Code, not data: the eight bytes of the third-column test of the sprite cell loop entered at $CE80 (outside this range) - it falls into the same tail at $CFF0 that draws the fourth column.

Paints a 2x2 block of 8x8 cells with the attribute byte in A and blanks their pixels, at the position held in $8027 (x) and $8028 (y). $D027 refuses any cell outside attribute page $5A with a row offset of $20-$DF and a column of 1-8, so the block only lands in the fixed window of screen rows 17-22, x 8-71. Callers are $CE79 with A=0 (erase it) and $CE82 with A=$20 (lay the background colour), at the start of each object the loop at $CEC0 then colours in.

One cell of the $CFF5 painter: writes attribute C to the cell at DE and sets that cell's eight pixel bytes to 0, so the cell becomes a block of the paper colour. It returns without touching anything unless DE is in attribute page $5A (screen rows 16-23) with a row offset of $20-$DF and a column of 1-8, which is what confines $CFF5 to its window.

24 bytes of state for the screen routine at $D05E: $D046/$D047 the pair of coordinates derived from $047 (D047 is $C0-ORed from $D046), $D048 a row counter, $D049-$D04D the bouncing vertical and horizontal velocities (read by the edge tests at $D102-$D12A), $D04F-$D054 three pairs of screen positions, $D057-$D059 the colour bytes that go with them and $D05A a flag.

Draws and runs the halt screen, reached only from $779A - the path taken at the start of a life when key-flag bit 4 of $8057 is set - and not executed in either snapshot, so what it looks like is open. It fills the attributes $5800-$5A1F with $55, marks both ends of attribute row 16 with $6D, maps the 30x8 pixel block at $5002 back over itself in reverse byte order through the table at $6200, lays the 8-byte columns of $D3EA/$D422 into screen columns 15 down to 2 with $D371, builds 1 KB of pattern at $FC00-$FFFF with $D37D, and then falls into the loop at $D0B5. That loop moves five objects (positions $D04F-$D054, velocities $D049-$D04D, colours $D057-$D059) and draws each with $D2A0, updating three derived positions with the maths at $D2C2; it ends at $D336 when a key is pressed.
Draws one object of the halt screen: complements the pattern byte $80BF, stores $AA AND that value in $80BE, then falls straight into $D2A0 to draw the object.

The halt screen's 'draw something at (D,E), height C' call: moves the previous frame's screen position into $801B/$801F/$801D, sets the new top-left corner in $8023/$8027, adds C to the bottom edge $8025 and tail-jumps into the sprite drawer at $900C. It is the same variable interface the game's object code fills in $DF44, so $D2A0 is how the halt screen calls the common drawing code.

Works out the three derived screen positions $D051, $D052 and $D054 that the halt screen loop draws at: for the angle in $D047 it takes three rounded sine/cosine offsets through the maths routine at $A8C4, scales each by $11, $22 and $1D with the multiply at $D320 and adds the base $D04A.
HL = A * DE, unsigned, by shift-and-add; A=0 returns 0 at once. Called by the halt screen's position code and from outside this range at $885A and $887A, so it is the game's shared 16x8 multiply.

The halt screen's wait-for-a-key test, also reached by the loop at $D16F: clicks through $E9E8, clears $8055 and reads the keyboard port $FE; with no key held it jumps back into the loop at $D0B5, and with a key held it falls through, fills the attributes from $5800 with $44, copies the bottom pixel row $57E0 over rows $50-$57 and calls $CE29 before returning.

Copies the eight bytes at (HL), one per pixel row $50-$57, down screen column E, then decrements E by one. Used with the pattern tables at $D3EA and $D422 to lay 8x8 tiles into the bottom third of the screen.

Writes exactly 1 KB of pattern to $FC00-$FFFF by pushing 2-byte words with the stack pointer set to $0000 - mostly $FFFF and $FFFE with a scatter of $xxAA/$xxFE - so it builds a 128x8 bitmap at the top of RAM. It keeps the old stack pointer in $E9E6 and restores it, and is called only from $D12F.

64 bytes of 8-pixel-high tiles for $D371: $D3EA-$D421 is seven 8-byte columns that the loop at $D073 draws into screen columns 15, 13, ... 3, and $D422-$D429 is one 8-byte column it draws again in every even column. The bytes are diagonal stripes ($AA, $FE, $A8, $FD, $FB, $A2, $EF, $8A); the picture they make on the halt screen is not established.

15 bytes of spawner state: $D42A the frame gap before the next object of the group, $D42B non-zero while a group is being spawned (set to $13 at $D616, cleared at $D68E), $D42C the 16-bit board-square pointer of the object being built, $D42E/$D42F its two spawn coordinates, $D430 the object's first byte, $D431 the direction flags, $D432 how many are still to be written, $D437 the frame gap of the type-$FB spawner at $D442.

Called once a frame from the main loop at $765F. It is the spawner for the extra hostile objects: it takes a random byte from $E472 and then, depending on $8068, the number of live objects in $7C71 and further random tests, appends 30-byte object records to the list whose end pointer is $7C72. The records are then handed to the walker at $D691.

Code, not data: the body of $D438 taken when $8068 is zero. Every tenth call ($D437 counts ten frames) it appends one 30-byte type-$FB record, up to thirteen records, holding $14 frames of life, start coordinates from $7FF5/$7FF7 and the speed pair $10,$10.

Second half of $D438, jumped to from $D43F. It does nothing with nine or more live objects; with exactly one live object, or when the random byte at $E46F equals $4E, it appends a type-$E5 record whose direction pair comes from the 5x5 table at $6432 through $DF9F, with the colours $0A and $CF/$D9, the record bytes +$0E..+$11 from $46F..471 and a last byte of $63.

Continuation of $D438 and the exit taken by the three early give-ups above. It takes a random byte and, when no group is in progress ($D42B zero), tests whether one may start: only when the angle byte $E470 has low six bits $19 and fewer than $0B objects are live does it search the 25-entry table at $6432 for a matching entry and spawn a group through $D586.
Code, not data: the two-instruction tail of the $6432 search at $D567 - the entry it wanted was found, so it jumps to $D586 to build the object.
Code, not data: the 'next table entry' step of the $6432 search at $D55A - it moves IX on by two bytes and loops through the 25 entries.

Entry to the spawn block taken when the $6432 search found a free entry: it saves the entry pointer in $D42C, works the new object's two screen coordinates $D42E/$D42F and the direction flags $D430/$D431 out of the entry's coordinate and size bytes, sets the group size from $E471 (1-4, stored in the object's +$16 and in $D432) and falls into $D634 to write the first record.
The in-group spawn tick, reached from $D531: decrements the frame gap $D42A and returns to the walker at $D691 while it is non-zero, otherwise falls into $D62E to write the next object of the group.

Writes one 30-byte object record at the end of the list: type $F1 (or $F0 for the head of the pair) at +0, the board-square pointer at +2, the two spawn coordinates at +5 and +7, the speed pair $0A,$0A at +8/+9, the two angles at +$0B and +$0D, the flags from $D431 at +$0E and +$13 xored with $80, and $FF/$00 at +$0F/+$10. It then advances $7C72 by 30 and decrements the group counter $D432, and at the end of the group clears $D42B so that $D52A may start another.

Walks the live object list for one frame. The list starts at $7C74, its end pointer is $7C72 and records are 30 bytes; the walk runs from the last record towards the first and each handler comes back through $D694 with HL holding the record it used. Type bytes $F3, $F1, $F0, $E3, $E5, $E6 and $FB go to $D6C9, $D9ED, $DB0C, $DAF1, $DC69, $DDF8 and $DE41; any other value drops through to $DEE6, which removes the record.
Code, not data: the last two comparisons of the dispatch chain at $D691 - type $FB to $DE41, otherwise on to the removal code.

Handler for the type-$F3 records, the objects that drive round the board. A negative countdown in the state byte +$12 (see $D6D3) is run down and ends by making the object a type-$E6 one; otherwise the step byte +$12 and turn rate +$13 are forced non-zero and the object is moved by $D6F4.
Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - the countdown in +$12, ending in the call to $DE22 that turns the object into a type-$E6 record.
Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - it makes sure the turn rate +$13 and the step byte +$12 are non-zero before the object moves.
Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - the second of the two 'make it non-zero' steps.
Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - the first of the two 'make it non-zero' steps, on the step byte +$12.
Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - it sets the step byte +$12 to 1 when it has run down to zero.

The movement of the type-$F3 objects: $DF04 works out the velocity from the two angles and $DFB8 reads the board square the object is over. If the square is off the board ($8028 is zero) the object goes to the reset at $D71E; if the last thing it hit was $FF ($803B) it goes to the collision response at $D845; and if the distance to that hit is under six units it goes to the steering at $D735.
Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - it limits the distance to the last hit to six and then steers.
Code, not data: the type-$F3 handler's 'left the board' path - it marks $803B and $8036 as $FF (nothing hit) and jumps to the reset at $D8BC.
Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - the path taken when nothing has been hit, comparing $803B with the level's byte at $7FFF before resetting.

Steering for the type-$F3 objects: it turns both angle bytes +$0B and +$0D away from the obstacle by the distance in C, steps the object's sub-position forward and back with $D97D and $D996, copies the board square into +$04..+$07 and looks the square up with $A192 into +$02. When the object has run off the board (through $D773) it counts its life +$17 down and, at the end, adds one to the counter $8066 and removes the record.
Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - the object's life counter +$17, which ends in a removal through $DEE6.

Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - it reloads the life counter +$17 with $28 and branches on bit 0 of +$15: the wander branch at $D7B3 turns the heading +$0E by the turn rate +$13 each frame (and flips sides when the random byte is $C6), and the other branch at $D7E4 is the attack behaviour.
Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - it flips bit 1 of the flags +$15 and the turn direction when the random byte is $C6.
Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - it adds the low five bits of the random byte to the accumulator +$14 and, when that overflows, reverses the turn rate +$13.

The attack branch of the type-$F3 objects: with bit 0 of +$15 clear it measures the distance to the target with $D941 and, when the object is close enough, locks on ($D7EB sets bit 0 of the flags +$01 and the $14-frame timer +$16); the other path counts that timer down and steers through $D818.
Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - it sets bit 0 of the record flags and the lock-on timer +$16 to $14.
Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - the lock-on test, using $D941's distance, the level byte $7FFF and bit 1 of +$15 to decide the turn direction handed to $D818.
Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - it keeps +$16 non-zero, compares the distance with the level byte $7FFF and sets or clears bit 1 of +$15.

The lock-on steering of the type-$F3 objects: it sets the timer +$16 and turns the heading +$0E towards the direction worked out from the collision bytes $803E and $8040, using the turn rate +$13 and $8024 to decide the sign.
Code, not data: the two bytes that pick between the two halves of the type-$F3 steering at $D83C.
Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - it adds the turn C to the heading +$0E (the entry points $D83A and $D83C differ only in the sign) and continues the walk at $D900.

The collision response of the type-$F3 objects, used when the thing hit was a type-$F1 object: it adds 20 to the counter $8060 and, if the object's life byte +$08 is $0E, it becomes a type-$E6 object (with +$08/+$09 set to $0A and the sound effect at $E4E8); otherwise ($D881) it is removed from the list straight away.
Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - the branch that removes the record and closes the gap in $7C71/$7C72.

Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - the path taken when the collision was not with a type-$F1 object: the object's y +$0B against $8036 decides between carrying on at $D746, the reset at $D8BC and the steering at $D738.
Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - the tail of the 'hit something else' test.

The reset path of the type-$F3 objects: zeroes $8033/$8035/$8037, recomputes the object's screen position with $DF44 and $DFB8, and then either falls into $D8E6 (nothing hit) or turns the distance to the hit into a steering step and goes back to $D735.
Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - the distance-to-steering conversion at the end of the reset path.
Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - with bit 0 of +$15 clear it snaps the heading +$0E to a multiple of $40 and runs the $D906 turn; with bit 0 set it goes to $D923 instead.

Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - the start of the grid-aligned turn: if the heading is already a multiple of $40 it goes straight to $D906, otherwise it snaps it and starts the nine-frame countdown +$18.
Code, not data: the common exit of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - it carries on the object walk at $D694 with the record just handled.
Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9 - it steps the heading by $40 a frame, counts +$18 down and at the end clears bit 1 of +$15 and restarts the timers.

Code, not data: part of the type-$F3 handler at $D6C9, entered with bit 0 of +$15 set - it adds the turn rate +$13 to the heading +$0E and then extends or retracts the object's sub-position with $D97D or $D996 according to the sign of +$13.

Returns HL as the distance of the object in IY from the target position at $7FF5/$7FF7: two absolute differences, each reduced by 2, added together, with the signed differences left in $803D and $803F. Used by the type-$F3 handler to decide whether the object is close enough to attack.

Adds $20 to each of the object's three sub-position bytes +$0F, +$10 and +$11 - one step of the object's sub-pixel position along its facing. Called from the movement code of the $F3 and $F1 handlers.
Subtracts 2 from each of the object's three sub-position bytes +$0F, +$10 and +$11; paired with $D97D, which adds $20 to the same three bytes, to make one step of the object's sub-pixel position.

Code, not data: part of the type-$F1 handler at $D9ED - the state +$0F = 0 branch: it counts the frame byte +$0E down and, when it runs out, moves the object seven units in both coordinates, recomputes its screen position and continues, or if it has left the board sets +$0B/+$0D to $FA and turns it into a type-$E6 object.

Handler for the type-$F1 records. It runs the reload byte +$10 down, wraps the animation byte +$0F from 4 back to 7, and then uses +$0F as an eight-way state: 0 steps and repositions the object ($D9A9), 1-3 set the step byte +$12 and continue into the movement at $DA18, $FD goes to $D9B2, $FE to $DA9D and $FF to $DB0F.

Handler for the type-$E3 records, dispatched from $D6B1: it counts +$17 down and then +$18, and when both are spent it adds +$16 to the counter at $8066 and removes the record - so an $E3 record pays out once its two timers run out.
Code, not data: the second half of the type-$E3 handler at $DAF1, where the two timers end in the add to $8066 and the removal at $DEE6.

Handler for the type-$F0 records, dispatched from $D6AC: it steps the animation byte +$14 down and, when that reaches zero, starts the object towards the target ($DB1F/$DB2B) and then tries to bring it onto the object it is chasing by reading that object's record through $8037 and adjusting $801B or $801D by half its size. The rest of the handler tests the object against the board and against whatever it has hit, with the fall-back at $DC4C that turns it back into a type-$F3 object.
Code, not data: the unreachable two bytes at $DBBD/$DBBA inside the type-$F0 handler at $DB0C - an 'inc (iy+$13)' wedged between two jumps.
Code, not data: the exit of the type-$F0 handler at $DB0C, which carries on the object walk, and the $DBC6 test of what the object is standing on.

Code, not data: part of the type-$F0 handler at $DB0C - the branch that hands the record back to the type-$F3 behaviour: type $F3, step +$12 = 4, turn rate +$13 = 6 and timers +$15/+$16 = 2, then steering away from the hit at $8036 through $D738.

Handler for the type-$E5 records, dispatched from $D6B6. It aims itself at the target: it compares its own coordinates with $7FF5/$7FF7, two 20-unit windows decide which axis it corrects, and the difference becomes a per-frame step in +$14/+$15 with the direction in +$16 and $8037, mirrored into $8033/$8035 for the board test. With both axes in range ($DCE4) it sets $8056 and writes the attribute $47 at $5AAA and $5A6A, then shortens +$0B/+$0D by five; if either borrows, the record becomes a type-$F3 object at $DD98.
Code, not data: part of the type-$E5 handler at $DC69 - the short fall-through between the axis test and the record-to-$F3 conversion.
Code, not data: the conversion at the end of the type-$E5 handler at $DC69 - +$0B/+$0D = $01/$0B, type $F3, +$18 = 2 and +$15 = 1.

Handler for the type-$E6 records, dispatched from $D6BB. It runs the life byte +$0E down from five and, as it falls, changes the sprite pointer +$0F/+$10 between the three tables at $C5EF, $C62B and $C5B3, so an $E6 record is the short animation left behind when an object is destroyed; when +$0E underflows the record is removed.
Code, not data: part of the type-$E6 handler at $DDF8 - the frame counter +$0E and the sprite pointer chosen by its value.

Turns the object in IY into a type-$E6 record: type $E6, life +$0E = 4, the sprite pointer $C5B3, and $08 written to both $8055 and $8056. Used from nine places in the object code as the 'this object has died' conversion.

Handler for the type-$FB records, dispatched from $D6C0. It counts the life byte at +1 down; on the last frame it sets $8055 to $21, removes the record and appends a new type-$F3 record built from the $FB record's own position and speed - so a $FB record is a delay marker that releases one moving object when it expires.
Code, not data: part of the type-$FB handler at $DE41 - the countdown of the life byte at +1 and its two early exits.

Counts the three-byte counter $BD6C-$BD6E up by one and plays the sound effect whose number that gives: while the low byte has not reached 10 it calls $BD12 with BC = the counter and A = the third byte. Called from $DBDA, so it is the 'play sound effect n' call made when an object is created.
Code, not data: part of the sound counter at $DEB8 - the carry from the second byte into the third and the call to $BD12.
Code, not data: part of the sound counter at $DEB8 - the store of the low byte and the call to $BD12 with the counter as its argument.

Removes the object in IY from the list: decrements the count $7C71, moves the end pointer $7C72 back by 30, copies every later record down over the one being removed with LDIR, and carries on the walk at $D694. This is what the handlers jump to when an object has died or gone off the board.

Turns the object's angle +$0E and step +$12 into a velocity: it takes the sine/cosine of the angle through $A8C4, scales it by the step with $A8D8, and leaves the two signed 16-bit results in $8035/$8037 and $8033 with their signs. Called by the $F3, $F1 and $F0 handlers before they move.

Works out where the object in IY sits on the board: it adds the step and the velocity to +$04..+$07, writes the four screen-position variables $801B, $8029, $801D and $802A that the drawing code reads, the two look-ahead values $801F/$8025 one step further on, the object's own position into $8023 and its two angles into $8021. Called from the movement code of every object handler, and also as the 'recompute after a reset' step.

HL = the word at $6432 + A * 10, i.e. entry A of the 25-entry 16-bit table at $6432, or HL unchanged (and the carry set) when A is 5 or more. The table at $6432 holds the pointers to the 30-byte board squares, so this maps a square number to its data; called by the spawner, the object handlers and $DFB8.

Clears the eight working variables $80A9-$80AF and $8035-$803B, then looks up four items in the 30-byte board square that $8021 points at - the square itself and its three neighbours, through $DF9F and the pointers at +0/+2/+4/+6 - keeping the four words in $80A9-$80AF and using them to fill the difference and speed variables $8024, $8036, $8027 and $803B. Called by every object handler before it tests the board.

The object code's overlap search, called four times by the block at $E0E7-$E109 with HL pointing at a board square's record list and BC = a value kept in $8049. It walks the records at a 7-byte stride from HL+8 until a zero byte, tests each record's stored coordinates against the current object's screen box ($801B, $801F, $801D, $8025) and keeps the best overlap in $8035..$803E, so the caller learns what the object has run into.
Code, not data: part of the overlap search at $E1CF - the case of a record whose flag byte has neither bit 6 nor bit 7 set.
Code, not data: part of the overlap search at $E1CF - the $C0 case of the record's flag byte, which takes the extent from the record's own first two bytes.
Code, not data: part of the overlap search at $E1CF - the $80 case of the record's flag byte.
Code, not data: part of the $80 case of the overlap search at $E1CF - it marks the current object's comparison byte in $8040 before the existing block is measured.
Code, not data: part of the $80 case of the overlap search at $E1CF - it measures the existing block through $908B.
Code, not data: part of the $80 case of the overlap search at $E1CF - the choice between the two stored positions before jumping into the common extent code at $E378.
Code, not data: part of the overlap search at $E1CF - the width and height of the overlapping block for the $80 case, measured through $9CCC.
Code, not data: part of the $80 case of the overlap search at $E1CF - it stores the measured position and the record's own first two bytes when bit 5 of the flag byte is set.
Code, not data: part of the overlap search at $E1CF - the $80 case's extents and the call to $9CCC that measures them.
Code, not data: the tail of the $80 case of the overlap search at $E1CF.

Code, not data: the shared part of the overlap search at $E1CF - it works the block's screen extent out with $908B and $9CCC and compares it with the current object's own box, keeping the largest overlap in $803B/$803D and the winning record's pointer and type in $8035/$8037/$8039.

Three bytes of pseudo-random state, $E46F, $E470 and $E471. Every call to $E472 advances them, and the code also reads the bytes directly as random values: $D4A1 compares $E46F with $4E, $D546 takes an index from its top bits and $D602 takes the spawn group size from $E471. $A451, $BE91 and $BE96 read $E46F outside this range.

Advances the three-byte state at $E46F-$E471 (shifting it left, folding the top bit back in, with an $A0 mask and $60 added on the way) and returns the new low byte in A. It is the game's pseudo-random source: callers write 'call $E472; cp $xx' to make a one-in-256 decision, so the same call also serves as a cheap clock for spawn timing.

Thirty-four descending bytes ($FF, $E6, $D2, $C5, $AA, $96, $82, down to $13, $12) indexed by an angle-like value that the code at $AC65 clamps to $1E before reading, and then passed to the maths routine at $A8DB - so this is the movement code's speed or falloff table, not note data.

The sound driver's state, three bytes: $E4AE/$E4AF the pointer to the script being played, $E4B0 the frames left on the current script step and $E4B1 the reload value for it. $E4F7/$E4FC start a script and $E9E8 reads one byte of it every frame.

Sound-effect scripts for the driver at $E9E8: a run of frame values, then a 0, then a two-byte pointer to the script to play next, so the scripts can be looped. This block ($E4B2-$E4E7) holds the three the game's own code uses internally.
Two short sound-effect scripts, $E4E8 and $E4EE, sharing one tail; $E4E8 is started from $D87B when an object is destroyed and $E4EE from the main loop at $7861.

Starts the sound effect whose script is at DE, but only if nothing is already playing: it returns at once when $E4B0 is non-zero, otherwise stores DE in $E4AE and sets the frame counter $E4B0/$E4B1 to $0101. Called from $7863, $9E8B, $A5F0, $A601 and $D87B.
The body of $E4F7 without the 'is something already playing' test: it stores DE in $E4AE and $0101 in $E4B0/$E4B1 so the script at DE begins on the next frame. Called directly from $7818.

Initialises the opening menu and starts its tune: it sets the sound counter $E4B0 to $0101, the script pointer $E4AE to $E4B2, prints message $86 and jumps into the music loop at $E69F, which never returns - the menu is read from inside the tune by the key handler at $E51C. Jumped to from $7F40 (straight after the picture copy), from $7699, $7899 and $78C6, and from $E57F when the key redefiner finishes.

The opening menu's key handler, called at the end of every note by the tone code at $E791. Key $23 starts a game (jumping to $757F), key $24 goes to the key redefiner at $E544, and key $1C toggles the input flag $E868 and redraws the menu with $E930.
Code, not data: part of the menu key handler at $E51C - the key $1C branch that toggles the input flag $E868 and redraws the menu.

The '1 REDEFINE KEYS' screen: it resets the stack to $F000, works through the nine key names in the 11-byte table at $E89B, waits for each new key with $7BE8 and $7B8B, stores it in the key table at $7BE0 and redraws that line, and when the ninth key is done it jumps back to the menu at $E508. Entered from the menu at $E529.
Code, not data: part of the key redefiner at $E544 - it returns to the menu at $E508 once the ninth key has been defined.

Waits until no key at all is held: it reads the keyboard port $FE, complements the five row bits and loops while any is set. Called between key redefinitions and at the mute points at $E540 and $E590.

HL = $E89B + A * 11, the address of entry A of the eleven-byte-per-entry key name table at $E89B ('>BLAST', ' BURP', ' FAST', ' SLOW', ' RIGHT', ' LEFT', ' BOUNC', ' ABORT', ' EXIT', each followed by the codes that colour it). Used by the key redefiner to point at the line it is rewriting.

The sound engine's data: twelve 16-bit note values at $E5CC-$E5E3 indexed by the note within the octave ($E716 shifts them for the octave), an eleven-entry table of 16-bit script pointers at $E5E4-$E5F9, and the tune's scripts from $E5FD to $E69E, which are runs of note bytes ending in $FF.

The title tune's top-level loop: it clears $E75D and repeatedly plays script $A0 through $E6AB, so the tune plays for as long as the menu is up. Reached from $E508 and from the end of a script at $E6A8; the keyboard is read from inside it by $E51C.

Plays one sound script: a command below $A0 is taken as a note, and $A0 and above index the eleven-entry pointer table at $E5E4, whose script is then read byte by byte - $FF ends and returns, $C8 repeats the rest with the mask $E75D flipped, and every other byte is played through $E716. Called from $E6A5, $E6D2 and $E6E1.
Code, not data: part of the sound script player at $E6AB - the $C8 command, which flips the mask at $E75D, plays the next byte and flips it back.
Code, not data: part of the sound script player at $E6AB - it plays the byte as a note and, for a repeat, calls itself for the sub-script.
Code, not data: part of the sound script player at $E6AB - it splits a note number into octave and note and decides whether to play it directly or through the second voice at $E6FC.

Turns the note number in A into the delay count the speaker loop needs: it takes that note's word from the table at $E5CC, shifts it by the octave count and leaves the result in HL (and DE), so this is the sound engine's pitch lookup. Called from the script player and from $E745.
Plays a note for a fixed length: it takes the delay from $E716, sets up the counter pair and falls into the tone loop at $E748.

Generates one tone on the speaker by toggling port $FE with the two counters HL and DE from $E716 as the delay, so the pitch comes from how fast this loop runs. Its inner count also reads the menu keys - it calls $E51C after every note - which is how the title tune doubles as the menu's idle loop. Called from the script player at $E705 and $E713 and from $E745.

The message pointer table and the messages it points at: nine 16-bit entries at $E795-$E7A6 ($E7A9 twice, $E7B1, $E7BD, $E7CA, $E7D2, $E7DB, $E882, $E92C) followed by the text with its control bytes. They read ‘CAPS SHIFT’, 'SYM SHIFT', 'ENTER', 'ENTER...', 'ER ...', the menu screen ('FAT WORM  BLOWS A SPARKY', a rule of underscores, 'BY JULIAN G TODD', 'DURELL SOFTWARE 1986', '1 REDEFINE KEYS', '0 START GAME', '2 KEMPSTON JOYSTICK') and the key redefiner ('KEY  REDEFINER', 'PRESS .. TO ADVANCE', 'PRESS .. TO CHANGE OR EXIT'). $E92C is a three-byte message of the character code $01 repeated.

Shows a full-screen text page: it rewrites 512 bytes of the attribute file from $5800 with $08 OR each cell's existing ink (the ink is kept and the paper forced to 1), clears $F000-$FFFF, and then prints the message numbered A with $E95D. Called with A=$86 and $87 by the menu and the key redefiner.

The text printer's state: $E95A/$E95B the cursor word (its low five bits are the column and the low three bits of its high byte are the row, bit-reversed), and $E95C the attribute byte written alongside each character.

Prints one character or a whole message. With bit 7 of A set it takes message A & $7F from the nine-entry pointer table at $E795 and walks that text, honouring $00 (end), $80 (the next word becomes the cursor, e.g. $F204) and $FE (the next byte becomes the attribute); with bit 7 clear it draws the character code in A. The cursor $E95A is not a screen address: the routine turns it into B = $58 or $59 and C = the cursor's low five bits ORed with the bit-reversed low three bits of its high byte, writes the attribute $E95C to that cell and to the cell 32 bytes on, then xors each of the eight ROM font bytes from $3C00 (each ORed with its own right shift) into the eight attribute cells down that column before stepping the cursor by one. Characters are taken from the ZX Spectrum ROM font at $3C00.
Two bytes where the stack pointer is kept while the code at $D37D, $E9E8 and $EAA9 uses the stack itself as a pattern filler and as the frame buffer.

Copies the off-screen frame buffer at $F000-$FFFF into the screen, xoring the ROM font in at $3C00 for any text wanted and clicking the speaker as it goes with a delay set from the frame byte $8055. It is also the sound effect player: it reads one byte per frame from the script at $E4AE with a countdown in $E4B0/$E4B1, so a script byte can hold a frame for several frames. Called every frame from $766B, $78EA, $790A, $7920, $D336 and $E956.
One byte, $C9, the 'ret' that ends the object renderer at $EAA9 standing alone after it.

Builds the off-screen frame: it fills $F000-$FFFF with $FFFF using the stack set to $0000 (clicking the speaker as it goes, with the delay counter $8056), then draws the nine object records at $8069 to $8099 through $EB2B. Called from the main loop at $7665, $78D3, $7904 and $791A, so this is the game's object renderer.

Draws one six-byte object record pointed at by HL: the two 16-bit coordinates go into $801B/$801F and $801D/$8025, and then it either clears that area with $8E13 (when the third word is zero) or draws the board square the word points at with $B350 and $B9F2 straight into the frame buffer. Called nine times from $EAA9 for the records at $8069-$8099.

$EB7E/$EB7F hold a 16-bit pointer used by the code at $9AB2 (which returns at once when the word is zero); $AAF9 clears it at the start of a game and $AAF3 stores the handler at $EB9C in the neighbouring pointer variable $8047.

Sixteen 16-bit values at $EB80-$EB9B: zero, $FFF8 twice, $0008 twice, zero, $0A0C and $FF and further bytes, small signed offsets that the pointer at $EB7E walks. The exact use is not established; the word at $EB7E is the only thing that refers to them, and $9AB5 stops as soon as that word is zero.

The level handler for the start of a game, and the routine whose address $AAF3 stores in the pointer variable $8047 (the indirect jumps to $8047 elsewhere all land here). It disables interrupts, sets the stack to $F000 and walks the 7-byte-stride table at $6464 looking for entries of type $F7 with the value $0C, choosing the board data at $BD6F, $BD90 or $BDD1 for each. The annotation stops at $EBCD because that is the end of this range; the routine continues past it.
